claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy has the typical microstructure of a homogenized solid solution.
Adding oxide nanoparticles will improve the alloy's high-temperature mechanical capability.
Adding oxide nanoparticles will not significantly increase alloy density.
Adding oxide nanoparticles will not compromise room-temperature performance.
The intervention is incorporation of approximately 1–2 vol% stable, high-melting-point oxide nanoparticles such as Y-Al-O.
The incorporated oxide particles will be uniformly distributed at grain boundaries and within grains.
The oxide particles will act as grain-boundary and intragranular pinning centers.
The oxide dispersoids impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
The oxide dispersoids restrict grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures.
Impeded dislocation motion and restricted grain-boundary sliding enhance creep resistance.
Impeded dislocation motion and restricted grain-boundary sliding enhance elevated-temperature yield strength.
The low oxide volume fraction minimizes adverse effects on room-temperature ductility.
The low oxide volume fraction minimizes the effect on density.
Above 800°C, the ODS-enhanced alloy will have 10–30% greater yield strength than the alloy without oxide nanoparticles.
Above 800°C, the ODS-enhanced alloy will have better creep resistance than the alloy without oxide nanoparticles.
The ODS-enhanced alloy will retain room-temperature performance comparable to the baseline alloy.
The ODS-enhanced alloy will have only a marginal density increase relative to the baseline alloy.
Excessive or poorly distributed oxide particles could reduce toughness.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with oxide type, particle distribution, and processing conditions.

A high-temperature yield-strength improvement below approximately 10%, a lack of meaningful creep-resistance improvement, or significant degradation of room-temperature performance would falsify the hypothesis.
